source: The same three macaque monkeys (MK1, MK2, MK3) participated in experiments 1 and 2, and a control experiment conducted in the absence of TUS.
evidence: Directly stated in the figure caption and experimental design description.

claim: Three other monkeys (MK4, MK5, MK6) participated in experiment 3.
source: Three other monkeys (MK4, MK5, MK6) participated in experiment 3.
evidence: Directly stated in the figure caption.

source: In all experiments anaesthesia was induced ~1.45 hr before the TUS intervention or no-TUS control.
evidence: Timing information provided in experimental design diagram.

claim: In experiment 1 the 40 s TUS protocol was delivered over the supplementary motor area (SMA).
source: In experiment 1 the 40 s TUS protocol was delivered over the supplementary motor area (SMA), while in experiments 2 and 3, the protocol was targeted at frontal polar cortex (FPC).

claim: In experiments 2 and 3, the TUS protocol was targeted at frontal polar cortex (FPC).
source: In experiment 1 the 40 s TUS protocol was delivered over the supplementary motor area (SMA), while in experiments 2 and 3, the protocol was targeted at frontal polar cortex (FPC).
evidence: Experimental design explicitly described in figure caption.

claim: Three consecutive runs of resting fMRI (26 min per run) were acquired starting ~40 min after the TUS or control protocol.
source: In all sessions, three consecutive runs of resting fMRI (26 min per run) were acquired starting ~40 min after the TUS or control protocol.

claim: TUS is a promising non-invasive brain stimulation technique.
source: Transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) is a promising non-invasive brain stimulation technique.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a characterization of TUS.

claim: To date, investigations report short-lived neuromodulatory effects of TUS.
source: To date, investigations report short-lived neuromodulatory effects, but to deliver on its full potential for research and therapy, ultrasound protocols are required that induce longer-lasting 'offline' changes.
evidence: Summary of prior literature on TUS effects.

claim: The TUS protocol presented modulates brain activation in macaques for more than one hour after 40 s of stimulation.
source: Here, we present a TUS protocol that modulates brain activation in macaques for more than one hour after 40 s of stimulation, while circumventing auditory confounds.

claim: The TUS protocol circumvents auditory confounds.
source: Here, we present a TUS protocol that modulates brain activation in macaques for more than one hour after 40 s of stimulation, while circumventing auditory confounds.
evidence: Stated as a feature of the protocol in the abstract.

claim: TUS caused stimulated areas to interact more selectively with the rest of the brain.
source: Normally activity in brain areas reflects activity in interconnected regions but TUS caused stimulated areas to interact more selectively with the rest of the brain.

claim: Regionally specific TUS effects were observed for two medial frontal brain regions – supplementary motor area and frontal polar cortex.
source: In a within-subject design, we observe regionally specific TUS effects for two medial frontal brain regions – supplementary motor area and frontal polar cortex.

claim: TUS induced signal changes in the meningeal compartment independently of site-specific effects.
source: Independently of these site-specific effects, TUS also induced signal changes in the meningeal compartment.

claim: TUS effects were temporary.
source: TUS effects were temporary and not associated with microstructural changes.

claim: TUS effects were not associated with microstructural changes.
source: TUS effects were temporary and not associated with microstructural changes.

claim: To understand brain circuits it is necessary both to record and manipulate their activity.
source: To understand brain circuits it is necessary both to record and manipulate their activity.

claim: Techniques for transiently manipulating activity in rodents, such as microstimulation, optogenetics, and chemogenetics, are increasingly accessible and applied.
source: While techniques for transiently manipulating activity in rodents, such as microstimulation, optogenetics, and chemogenetics (Sternson and Roth, 2014; Vanduffel, 2016), are increasingly accessible and applied, techniques for manipulating activity in the primate brain are less widely available and remain accessible to comparatively few researchers in a limited number of research centres worldwide (Galvan et al., 2018; Krug et al., 2015; Vanduffel, 2016).
evidence: Statement about current state of neuroscience techniques with citations.

claim: Techniques for manipulating activity in the primate brain are less widely available and remain accessible to comparatively few researchers in a limited number of research centres worldwide.
source: While techniques for transiently manipulating activity in rodents, such as microstimulation, optogenetics, and chemogenetics (Sternson and Roth, 2014; Vanduffel, 2016), are increasingly accessible and applied, techniques for manipulating activity in the primate brain are less widely available and remain accessible to comparatively few researchers in a limited number of research centres worldwide (Galvan et al., 2018; Krug et al., 2015; Vanduffel, 2016).
evidence: Statement about limitations of primate neuroscience with citations.

claim: A prominent limitation for many brain stimulation tools is the duration of the induced neuromodulatory effects, often not outlasting the stimulation by more than a few seconds or minutes.
source: A prominent limitation for many brain stimulation tools for research and therapeutic interventions is the duration of the induced neuromodulatory effects, often not outlasting the stimulation by more than a few seconds or minutes.
evidence: Statement about limitations of existing brain stimulation techniques.

claim: The particular protocol of low intensity pulsed transcranial focused ultrasound stimulation (TUS) induces a sustained period of neuromodulation in primates without inducing structural damage.
source: Here we report on a particular protocol of low intensity pulsed transcranial focused ultrasound stimulation (TUS) that we show induces a sustained period of neuromodulation in primates without inducing structural damage.
evidence: Main claim of the study stated in introduction.

claim: TUS can be applied in the absence of a craniotomy.
source: The TUS approach in general is a relatively new one (Dallapiazza et al., 2018; Tufail et al., 2011; Tyler et al., 2018; Yoo et al., 2011; Younan et al., 2013) and like transcranial magnetic stimulation (Dayan et al., 2013) and transcranial electric stimulation (Polanía et al., 2018) it can be applied in the absence of a craniotomy.
evidence: Characteristic of TUS stated with citations.

claim: In vitro recordings have identified several mechanisms by which ultrasound stimulation could affect neurons.
source: In vitro recordings have identified several mechanisms by which ultrasound stimulation could affect neurons.

claim: It has been proposed that the sound pressure wave exerts a mechanical effect on neuronal activity through ion channel gating and changes to the membrane capacitance.
source: It has been proposed that the sound pressure wave exerts a mechanical effect on neuronal activity through ion channel gating and changes to the membrane capacitance (Blackmore et al., 2018; Kubanek et al., 2018; Kubanek et al., 2016; Prieto et al., 2013).

claim: TUS may be suitable as a tool for focal manipulation of activity in many brain areas in primates.
source: While the precise mechanism is being determined, early applications, including the current results, suggest TUS may be suitable as a tool for focal manipulation of activity in many brain areas in primates (Fomenko et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2016a; Legon et al., 2018; Munoz et al., 2018; Naor et al., 2016; Tufail et al., 2011; Tyler et al., 2018; Yoo et al., 2011).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from prior work and current results with citations.

claim: TUS application over the frontal eye field (FEF) affects the same aspects of oculomotor behaviour that are compromised by FEF lesion, whilst leaving intact those aspects of oculomotor behaviour that are unaffected by FEF lesion.
source: In the macaque, its application over the frontal eye field (FEF) affects the same aspects of oculomotor behaviour that are compromised by FEF lesion, whilst leaving intact those aspects of oculomotor behaviour that are unaffected by FEF lesion (Deffieux et al., 2013).
evidence: Prior finding in macaques with citation.

claim: Pioneering work in humans has focused on modulating and eliciting evoked responses by focused ultrasound in both cortical and subcortical sensorimotor regions.
source: Pioneering work in humans has focused on modulating and eliciting evoked responses by focused ultrasound in both cortical and subcortical sensorimotor regions (Lee et al., 2016a; Lee et al., 2015; Legon et al., 2018; Legon et al., 2014).
evidence: Summary of prior human studies with citations.

claim: To date ultrasonic applications are primarily focused on direct 'online' effects.
source: To date ultrasonic applications are primarily focused on direct 'online' effects.
evidence: Statement about current state of TUS research.

claim: Some studies have observed neuromodulatory effects outlasting the sonication by several minutes before returning to baseline, with more pronounced effects for protocols delivered at higher intensities (Isppa >5 W/cm2) and higher duty cycles (>5%).
source: Nonetheless, some studies have observed neuromodulatory effects outlasting the sonication by several minutes before returning to baseline, with more pronounced effects for protocols delivered at higher intensities (Isppa >5 W/cm2) and higher duty cycles (>5%; Kim et al., 2015; Yoo et al., 2011).
evidence: Summary of prior findings with citations and specific parameters.

claim: Following ultrasound protocols with a relatively high rate of acoustic energy deposition, the neuromodulatory effects outlast the sonication period for up to 10 min following 43.7 ms long 1.14MHz pulses repeated at 10 Hz for 40 s.
source: For example, following ultrasound protocols with a relatively high rate of acoustic energy deposition, characterized by pulses tens of milliseconds long, repeated at 10 Hz, the neuromodulatory effects outlast the sonication period: for up to 10 min following 43.7 ms long 1.14MHz pulses repeated at 10 Hz for 40 s (Dallapiazza et al., 2018), or for up to 20 min following 30 ms long 350 kHz pulses repeated at 10 Hz for 40 s (Ahnine et al., 2018).
evidence: Specific prior finding with citation and protocol details.

claim: Following ultrasound protocols with a relatively high rate of acoustic energy deposition, the neuromodulatory effects outlast the sonication period for up to 20 min following 30 ms long 350 kHz pulses repeated at 10 Hz for 40 s.
source: For example, following ultrasound protocols with a relatively high rate of acoustic energy deposition, characterized by pulses tens of milliseconds long, repeated at 10 Hz, the neuromodulatory effects outlast the sonication period: for up to 10 min following 43.7 ms long 1.14MHz pulses repeated at 10 Hz for 40 s (Dallapiazza et al., 2018), or for up to 20 min following 30 ms long 350 kHz pulses repeated at 10 Hz for 40 s (Ahnine et al., 2018).
evidence: Specific prior finding with citation and protocol details.

claim: Recent work has highlighted the possibility that in rodents some TUS protocols can evoke a startle response when the stimulation is modulated at audible frequencies.
source: Recent work has highlighted the possibility that in rodents some TUS protocols can evoke a startle response when the stimulation is modulated at audible frequencies (Guo et al., 2018; Sato et al., 2018).
evidence: Summary of recent findings with citations.

claim: The auditory effect of TUS is limited to the stimulation period and dissipates within 75 ms to 4 s.
source: Importantly, this auditory effect is limited to the stimulation period and dissipates within 75 ms to 4 s.
evidence: Temporal characteristic of auditory confound from prior work.

claim: In more deeply anaesthetized animals, when the intrinsic neural activity of a system is suppressed, some TUS protocols might fail to evoke action potentials at the site of stimulation.
source: This work has also emphasized that in more deeply anaesthetized animals, when the intrinsic neural activity of a system is suppressed, some TUS protocols might fail to evoke action potentials at the site of stimulation.
evidence: Finding from prior work about anaesthesia effects.

claim: TUS' actions might be primarily neuromodulatory in nature and/or most prominently observable when they interact with ongoing physiological activity.
source: This suggests TUS' actions might be primarily neuromodulatory in nature and/or that they are most prominently observable when they interact with ongoing physiological activity.

claim: The impact that any stimulation protocol might have will be a function of the animal model being used and the precise details of the ultrasound frequencies, pulse shape, protocol, and ongoing brain activity.
source: However, as has been noted (Airan and Butts Pauly, 2018) the impact that any stimulation protocol might have, will be a function of the animal model being used and the precise details of the ultrasound frequencies, pulse shape, protocol, and ongoing brain activity.

claim: With the offline protocol and anaesthesia regime used, the study controls for potential auditory artefacts and shows that TUS has an effect that cannot be attributed to them.
source: With the offline protocol and anaesthesia regime we used we control for such potential artefacts and show that TUS has an effect that cannot be attributed to them.
evidence: Claim about the study's experimental design and findings.

claim: The study focused on the effects of TUS outlasting the stimulation period, investigating the impact of 40 s trains of TUS on measurements of neural activity in three macaque monkeys provided by fMRI up to 2 hr after stimulation.
source: Here we focused on the effects of TUS outlasting the stimulation period, investigating the impact of 40 s trains of TUS on measurements of neural activity in three macaque monkeys provided by functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) up to 2 hr after stimulation (Figure 1, top panel).
evidence: Description of study design and methods.

claim: FMRI is one of the most widely used methods for estimating neural activity.
source: FMRI is one of the most widely used methods for estimating neural activity.
evidence: Statement about fMRI as a method.

claim: Despite limitations in its spatial and temporal resolution, fMRI remains important because it is non-invasive and can often be used to provide information about activity throughout the whole brain.
source: Despite limitations in its spatial and temporal resolution, fMRI remains important because it is non-invasive and can often be used to provide information about activity throughout the whole brain.

claim: FMRI provides an estimate of how activity changes in tandem with sensory, cognitive, or motor events or with activity in another brain region rather than a direct measure of neural activity.
source: Rather than providing a direct measure of neural activity, however, it provides an estimate of how activity changes in tandem with sensory, cognitive, or motor events or with activity in another brain region.

claim: FMRI-measured activity in any given brain area is a function of activity in other brain areas, especially those with which it is closely interconnected.
source: Typically, fMRI-measured activity in any given brain area is a function of activity in other brain areas, especially those with which it is closely interconnected (Neubert et al., 2015; O'Reilly et al., 2013).
evidence: Principle of fMRI connectivity with citations.

claim: Although many brain areas may share any given individual connection, the overall pattern of connections of each area is unique.
source: Although many brain areas may share any given individual connection (for example both areas A and B may project to C), the overall pattern of connections of each area is unique (Passingham et al., 2002); as such, the overall pattern of connections therefore constitutes a 'connectional fingerprint'.
evidence: Concept of connectional fingerprint with citation.

claim: It is possible to use fMRI measurements of correlations in the BOLD signal across brain regions to estimate the connectivity fingerprints of a given brain area.
source: As a result it is possible to use fMRI measurements of correlations in the blood oxygen level dependent (BOLD) signal across brain regions to estimate the connectivity fingerprints of a given brain area (Figure 1, bottom right panel; Caspari et al., 2018; Ghahremani et al., 2017; Margulies et al., 2016, Margulies et al., 2009; Mars et al., 2013; Sallet et al., 2013; Shen, 2015; Shen et al., 2015).
evidence: Method for estimating connectivity fingerprints with citations.

claim: Activity in any given brain area is a function of the activity in the areas with which it is interconnected.
source: This implies that activity in any given brain area is a function of the activity in the areas with which it is interconnected.

claim: Simulations showed the study was able to selectively target SMA and FPC.
source: Simulations showed we were able to selectively target these regions (Figure 2; see Acoustic and thermal modelling for more details).

claim: SMA and FPC have distinct anatomical and functional connections.
source: These regions have distinct anatomical and functional connections; SMA is most strongly coupled with the sensorimotor system, while the FPC interacts primarily with the prefrontal cortex and only interacts indirectly with the sensorimotor system via SMA (Petrides and Pandya, 2007; Sallet et al., 2013).
evidence: Characterization of brain regions with citations.

claim: SMA is most strongly coupled with the sensorimotor system.
source: These regions have distinct anatomical and functional connections; SMA is most strongly coupled with the sensorimotor system, while the FPC interacts primarily with the prefrontal cortex and only interacts indirectly with the sensorimotor system via SMA (Petrides and Pandya, 2007; Sallet et al., 2013).
evidence: Characterization of SMA connectivity with citations.

claim: FPC interacts primarily with the prefrontal cortex and only interacts indirectly with the sensorimotor system via SMA.
source: These regions have distinct anatomical and functional connections; SMA is most strongly coupled with the sensorimotor system, while the FPC interacts primarily with the prefrontal cortex and only interacts indirectly with the sensorimotor system via SMA (Petrides and Pandya, 2007; Sallet et al., 2013).
evidence: Characterization of FPC connectivity with citations.

claim: In the control state, each area's activity is normally a function of the activity in the areas that constitute its connectional fingerprint.
source: In the control state, each area's activity is normally a function of the activity in the areas that constitute its connectional fingerprint.

claim: If the pattern of activity coupling is altered by TUS in a manner that is dependent on the location of the stimulation, then this will constitute evidence that TUS exerts a spatially selective effect on neural activity.
source: If this pattern is altered by TUS in a manner that is dependent on the location of the stimulation, then this will constitute evidence that TUS exerts a spatially selective effect on neural activity.
evidence: Logical criterion for demonstrating spatial specificity.

claim: In a within-subject design, the same three animals participated in experiments 1 and 2, and a control experiment conducted in the absence of TUS.
source: In a within-subject design, the same three animals participated in experiments 1 and 2, and a control experiment conducted in the absence of TUS (Figure 1).

claim: FMRI was acquired in three conditions for all animals: following SMA TUS, following FPC TUS, and in a control state.
source: As such, fMRI was acquired in three conditions for all animals: following SMA TUS, following FPC TUS, and in a control state.

claim: Each of the MRI sessions consisted of three consecutive runs.
source: In turn, each of the MRI sessions consisted of three consecutive runs.

claim: The results of experiment two were validated in a new set of three different animals (experiment 3).
source: We also validated the results of experiment two in a new set of three different animals (experiment 3).

claim: Ultrasound modulation of SMA and FPC led to focal, area-specific changes in each stimulated region's connectivity profile.
source: Ultrasound modulation of SMA and FPC led to focal, area-specific changes in each stimulated region's connectivity profile.

claim: In each area, a region's activity pattern after TUS application was more a function of its own activity and that of strongly connected regions, but less a function of activity in more remote and weakly interconnected areas.
source: In each area, a region's activity pattern after TUS application was more a function of its own activity and that of strongly connected regions, but less a function of activity in more remote and weakly interconnected areas.
evidence: Description of TUS effects on connectivity.

claim: Independent of specific grey matter signal changes, TUS also interacted with non-neuronal structures, as evidenced by more widespread signal changes observed in the meningeal compartment.
source: Independent of these specific grey matter signal changes, TUS also interacted with non-neuronal structures, as evidenced by more widespread signal changes observed in the meningeal compartment (including cerebral spinal fluid and vasculature).

claim: In experiment four, TUS application had no observable impact on cortical microstructure apparent on histological examination.
source: Finally, in experiment four we demonstrate that TUS application had no observable impact on cortical microstructure apparent on histological examination.

claim: TUS over dorsomedial frontal cortex causes spatially specific sharpening of the stimulated region's connectivity profile with high efficacy and reproducibility, independent of non-neuronal signal changes.
source: In summary, TUS over dorsomedial frontal cortex causes spatially specific sharpening of the stimulated region's connectivity profile with high efficacy and reproducibility, independent of non-neuronal signal changes.

claim: Transcranial focused ultrasound stimulation of SMA induced spatially specific changes to the connectivity profile of SMA.
source: Transcranial focused ultrasound stimulation of SMA induced spatially specific changes to the connectivity profile of SMA.

claim: At rest, in the control state, SMA's activity is coupled with activity throughout sensorimotor regions in frontal and parietal cortex, inferior parietal, prefrontal, and parts of cingulate cortex.
source: At rest, in the control state, SMA's activity is coupled with activity throughout sensorimotor regions in frontal and parietal cortex, inferior parietal, prefrontal, and parts of cingulate cortex (Figure 3a).
evidence: Baseline connectivity pattern shown in data.

claim: Many of the regions coupled with SMA are anatomically connected with SMA.
source: Many of these regions are anatomically connected with SMA (Dum and Strick, 2005; Geyer et al., 2000; Strick et al., 1998).
evidence: Anatomical basis for functional connectivity with citations.

claim: Following ultrasound stimulation, SMA changed its coupling with the sensorimotor system, anterior and posterior cingulate, anterior temporal, inferior parietal, and prefrontal cortex.
source: Following ultrasound stimulation, SMA changed its coupling with the sensorimotor system, anterior and posterior cingulate, anterior temporal, inferior parietal, and prefrontal cortex (Figure 3b).

claim: Compared to the control state, after TUS over SMA, SMA's positive coupling is enhanced with proximal areas in the sensorimotor system but reduced in many long-range connections.
source: Compared to the control state (blue line), after TUS over SMA (red line), SMA's positive coupling is enhanced with proximal areas in the sensorimotor system but reduced in many long-range connections (non-parametric permutation test, p=0.017).

claim: The primary motor cortex (M1), superior parietal lobe (SPL), and middle cingulate cortex (MCC) in the dorsomedial sensorimotor network have been reported to be closely connected with the SMA.
source: The primary motor cortex (M1), superior parietal lobe (SPL), and middle cingulate cortex (MCC) in the dorsomedial sensorimotor network have been reported to be closely connected with the SMA, whereas prefrontal regions on the dorsomedial (area 9m and FPC), dorsolateral (areas 9-46d and 8A), and ventromedial (area 11m) surface, and those in the temporal lobe (anterior superior temporal gyrus, aSTG; middle superior temporal sulcus, midSTS), and parietal cortex (caudal inferior parietal lobule, IPLc; posterior parietal cortex, PCC) have been reported to be less closely connected with the SMA (Dum and Strick, 2005; Geyer et al., 2000; Strick et al., 1998).
evidence: Anatomical connectivity patterns from literature with citations.

claim: Prefrontal regions on the dorsomedial, dorsolateral, and ventromedial surface, and those in the temporal lobe and parietal cortex have been reported to be less closely connected with the SMA.
source: The primary motor cortex (M1), superior parietal lobe (SPL), and middle cingulate cortex (MCC) in the dorsomedial sensorimotor network have been reported to be closely connected with the SMA, whereas prefrontal regions on the dorsomedial (area 9m and FPC), dorsolateral (areas 9-46d and 8A), and ventromedial (area 11m) surface, and those in the temporal lobe (anterior superior temporal gyrus, aSTG; middle superior temporal sulcus, midSTS), and parietal cortex (caudal inferior parietal lobule, IPLc; posterior parietal cortex, PCC) have been reported to be less closely connected with the SMA (Dum and Strick, 2005; Geyer et al., 2000; Strick et al., 1998).
evidence: Anatomical connectivity patterns from literature with citations.

claim: TUS increased positive coupling between the stimulated area and proximal areas normally closely connected with it, while decreasing coupling between the stimulated area and many areas normally less closely connected with it.
source: TUS increased positive coupling between the stimulated area and proximal areas normally closely connected with it, while, at the same time, decreasing coupling between the stimulated area and many areas normally less closely connected with it.
evidence: Summary of TUS effects on connectivity.

claim: The specific effects of TUS were sustained over the duration of the experiment, lasting up to 2 hr.
source: These specific effects of TUS were sustained over the duration of our experiment, lasting up to 2 hr (Figure 5d–f).
evidence: Temporal extent of effects shown in data.

claim: Disruptive effects of TUS on long-range coupling were especially prominent immediately following the end of TUS application and gradually reduced towards the end of the recording session.
source: Disruptive effects of TUS on long-range coupling were especially prominent immediately following the end of TUS application (Figure 5d), and gradually reduced towards the end of our recording session (Figure 5f).
evidence: Time course of effects shown in data.

claim: The enhancing effects that TUS exerted on SMA's coupling with adjacent and strongly connected areas had a relatively delayed appearance, arising well after the TUS had ended (more than 1 hr), but again decreasing towards the end of the recording session.
source: The enhancing effects that TUS exerted on SMA's coupling with adjacent and strongly connected areas had a relatively delayed appearance, arising well after the TUS had ended (more than 1 hr, Figure 5e), but again decreasing towards the end of the recording session.
evidence: Time course of enhancement effects shown in data.

claim: The observed pattern could signify distinct time courses for TUS-induced long-term depression and long-term potentiation.
source: While we are cautious about overinterpreting precise timing differences between long-range connectivity reductions and local connectivity increments, we note that the observed pattern could signify distinct time courses for TUS-induced long-term depression and long-term potentiation.

claim: The observed pattern is consistent with the notion that early disruption of long-range input to a network leaves relatively more signal variance in this network to be explained by remaining local input, driving the observation of subsequent within-network coupling increments.
source: However, the observed pattern is also consistent with the notion that early disruption of long-range input to a network (Figure 5d) leaves relatively more signal variance in this network to be explained by remaining local input, driving the observation of subsequent within-network coupling increments (Figure 5e).

claim: Both proposed mechanisms would lead to a sharpening of the stimulated region's connectivity profile, as observed.
source: Both these mechanisms would lead to a sharpening of the stimulated region's connectivity profile, as observed here.
evidence: Conclusion about mechanisms consistent with observations.

claim: FPC's activity is coupled with that in interconnected brain regions even when animals are at rest in the control state.
source: Like SMA, FPC's activity is coupled with that in interconnected brain regions even when animals are at rest in the control state (Figure 3d).
evidence: Baseline connectivity pattern shown in data.

claim: FPC's activity is positively correlated with activity in a number of adjacent dorsomedial and lateral prefrontal areas and in the central portion of the superior temporal sulcus (midSTS) and posterior cingulate cortex with which it is monosynaptically interconnected.
source: FPC's activity is positively correlated with activity in a number of adjacent dorsomedial and lateral prefrontal areas and in the central portion of the superior temporal sulcus (midSTS) and posterior cingulate cortex with which it is monosynaptically interconnected (Petrides and Pandya, 2007).
evidence: Connectivity pattern with anatomical basis and citation.

claim: At rest, there was a negative relationship between FPC activity and activity in sensorimotor areas, with which FPC is indirectly connected via regions such as SMA.
source: By contrast there was, at a rest, a negative relationship with the activity in sensorimotor areas, with which FPC is indirectly connected via regions such as SMA.

claim: In comparison to the control state, FPC stimulation induced an enhancement in the normal short-range connectivity between FPC and adjacent dorsomedial and lateral prefrontal cortex with which it is particularly strongly connected.
source: In comparison to the control state, FPC stimulation induced an enhancement in the normal short-range connectivity between FPC and adjacent dorsomedial (area 9m) and lateral prefrontal cortex (area 9-46d) with which it is particularly strongly connected.

claim: FPC TUS induced a similar enhancement effect in more distant regions with which FPC is strongly connected – the midSTS, IPLc and PCC, together comprising temporal and parietal segments of the primate 'default mode network'.
source: In addition, a similar effect was seen in more distant regions with which it is also strongly connected – the midSTS, IPLc and PCC, together comprising temporal and parietal segments of the primate 'default mode network' (Petrides and Pandya, 2007).
evidence: TUS effect on long-range connectivity with citation.

claim: FPC TUS led to reduced coupling with areas in prefrontal cortex that FPC is connected to but less strongly, including ventromedial, subgenual cingulate, and lateral orbitofrontal cortex.
source: By contrast, there was reduced coupling with other areas in prefrontal cortex, including ventromedial (area 14m), subgenual cingulate (area 25), and lateral orbitofrontal cortex (area 47-12o). These are all areas that FPC is connected to but less strongly (Petrides and Pandya, 2007).
evidence: TUS effect on weakly connected regions with citation.

claim: TUS applied to FPC led to a change in long-range connectivity between FPC and several motor association regions with which it is not directly connected, especially those in the ventrolateral parieto-frontal sensorimotor network.
source: Finally, TUS applied to FPC also led to a change in long-range connectivity between FPC and several motor association regions with which it is not directly connected, especially those in the ventrolateral parieto-frontal sensorimotor network (areas PF and F4 Petrides and Pandya, 2007).
evidence: TUS effect on indirect connections with citation.

claim: In the control state, the activity in FPC and sensorimotor association areas is negatively or anti-correlated, but this anti-correlation was reduced by FPC TUS.
source: As noted, in the control state, the activity in FPC and these sensorimotor association areas is negatively or anti-correlated, but this anti-correlation was reduced by FPC TUS.

claim: FPC TUS significantly altered FPC functional connectivity.
source: Although FPC TUS significantly altered FPC functional connectivity, it had comparatively little impact on SMA's pattern of functional connectivity; there was no difference in SMA's functional connectivity between the control state and after FPC TUS (non-parametric permutation test, p=0.231; whole-brain map in Figure 3c and yellow line in connectivity fingerprint in Figure 5a).
evidence: Statistical finding about FPC TUS effects.

claim: FPC TUS had comparatively little impact on SMA's pattern of functional connectivity; there was no difference in SMA's functional connectivity between the control state and after FPC TUS.
source: Although FPC TUS significantly altered FPC functional connectivity, it had comparatively little impact on SMA's pattern of functional connectivity; there was no difference in SMA's functional connectivity between the control state and after FPC TUS (non-parametric permutation test, p=0.231; whole-brain map in Figure 3c and yellow line in connectivity fingerprint in Figure 5a).

claim: The effects of TUS over SMA on SMA's connectivity were significantly dissociable from the effects of FPC TUS.
source: Importantly, the effects of TUS over SMA on SMA's connectivity were significantly dissociable from the effects of FPC TUS (non-parametric permutation test, p=0.041).
evidence: Statistical finding about dissociability of effects.

claim: SMA TUS had some but comparatively little impact on FPC's pattern of functional connectivity.
source: Similarly, SMA TUS had some but comparatively little impact on FPC's pattern of functional connectivity (non-parametric permutation tests, SMA versus control, p=0.047; SMA versus FPC, p=0.028; whole-brain map in Figure 3e and red line in connectivity fingerprint in Figure 5b).

claim: The most prominent changes in FPC's connectional fingerprint induced by SMA stimulation were the disruption of functional connectivity between FPC and sensorimotor areas.
source: In fact, the most prominent changes in each area's connectional fingerprint that were induced by stimulation of the other area were the disruption of functional connectivity between FPC and sensorimotor areas when SMA was stimulated (Figure 3e, encircled).
evidence: Specific cross-site effect observed in data.

claim: FPC has no direct monosynaptic connections with sensorimotor areas.
source: This particular result may have occurred because, as already noted, FPC has no direct monosynaptic connections with these sensorimotor areas (Petrides and Pandya, 2007) and so its functional coupling with these areas is likely to be mediated by areas such as SMA and the areas that surround it such as the pre-supplementary motor area and the cingulate motor areas (Bates and Goldman-Rakic, 1993; Lu et al., 1994).

claim: FPC's functional coupling with sensorimotor areas is likely to be mediated by areas such as SMA and the areas that surround it such as the pre-supplementary motor area and the cingulate motor areas.
source: This particular result may have occurred because, as already noted, FPC has no direct monosynaptic connections with these sensorimotor areas (Petrides and Pandya, 2007) and so its functional coupling with these areas is likely to be mediated by areas such as SMA and the areas that surround it such as the pre-supplementary motor area and the cingulate motor areas (Bates and Goldman-Rakic, 1993; Lu et al., 1994).
evidence: Inference about connectivity mediation with citations.

claim: SMA TUS only affects FPC coupling with SMA itself and the regions which are coupled with FPC only through SMA.
source: In fact, these circumscribed exceptions may well confirm the rule that a region's connectivity pattern is only affected by stimulation of the region itself. Namely, SMA TUS only affects FPC coupling with SMA itself and the regions which are coupled with FPC only through SMA.

claim: The effects of TUS in different frontal regions were clearly dissociable.
source: In conclusion, the effects of TUS in different frontal regions were clearly dissociable.

claim: The reproducibility of TUS effects was investigated by examining the impact of TUS to FPC in three additional individuals in a biological replication experiment (experiment 3).
source: We investigated the reproducibility of TUS effects by examining the impact of TUS to FPC in three additional individuals in a biological replication experiment (experiment 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: In experiment 3, TUS had the same effects as seen in experiment 2: a site-specific sharpening of the stimulated region's connectional profile.
source: TUS had the same effects as seen in experiment 2: a site-specific sharpening of the stimulated region's connectional profile.

claim: The observed sharpening in experiment 3 was less prominently related to activity coupling decreases than in experiment 2.
source: Notwithstanding, when reviewing the simple effects driving the well-matched interaction, we note that the observed sharpening was less prominently related to activity coupling decreases in experiment 3 than in experiment 2.

claim: Subjects used in experiment 2 and 3 did not differ regarding depth of anaesthesia or duration between sedation and fMRI data collection.
source: However, subjects used in experiment 2 and 3 did not differ regarding depth of anaesthesia or duration between sedation and fMRI data collection.

claim: It has been suggested that certain TUS protocols might have a limited efficacy in evoking spiking activity at the stimulation site, but rather exert their influence on the brain through the auditory system, not unlike an auditory startle response.
source: It has recently been suggested that certain TUS protocols might have a limited efficacy in evoking spiking activity at the stimulation site, but rather exert their influence on the brain through the auditory system, not unlike an auditory startle response (Guo et al., 2018; Sato et al., 2018).
evidence: Summary of concerns from prior work with citations.

claim: The efficacy of TUS may be a function of both the specifics of the stimulation protocol and of ongoing neural activity.
source: First, it is possible that the efficacy of TUS is a function of both the specifics of the stimulation protocol and of ongoing neural activity.
evidence: Proposed explanation for variable TUS effects.

claim: A neuromodulatory technique may fail to elicit spiking activity in deeply anaesthetized rodents.
source: A neuromodulatory technique may fail to elicit spiking activity in deeply anaesthetized rodents (Guo et al., 2018; Sato et al., 2018).

claim: Whole-brain functional connectivity, as measured with the BOLD signal, is preserved at the anaesthesia levels used in this study.
source: Importantly, it is known that whole-brain functional connectivity, as measured with the BOLD signal, is preserved at these levels (Mars et al., 2013; Neubert et al., 2015; Neubert et al., 2014; O'Reilly et al., 2013; Sallet et al., 2013; Vincent et al., 2007).
evidence: Justification for anaesthesia protocol with citations.

claim: TUS modulated the activity coupling of each stimulated area in a regionally specific manner under the conditions used.
source: Under these distinct conditions, we observed that TUS modulated the activity coupling of each stimulated area in a regionally specific manner.
evidence: Summary of findings under specific experimental conditions.

claim: TUS induced more spatially homogenous activation within the stimulated area, but not in the non-stimulated region.
source: This analysis revealed that TUS induced more spatially homogenous activation within the stimulated area, but not in the non-stimulated region (interaction of TUS x connectivity seed: F(1,8)=1571.2, p=1.8044e-10, d = 11.4426, CI=[1.2733 1.1333]).

claim: The effect of TUS on spatial homogeneity of the signal was not accompanied by changes to the temporal variance of the BOLD signal fluctuations in the stimulated or other regions.
source: This effect on spatial homogeneity of the signal was not accompanied by changes to the temporal variance of the BOLD signal fluctuations in the stimulated or other regions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Finding about temporal variance with figure reference.

claim: The standard deviation of the BOLD signal fluctuations over time were strikingly similar between the two stimulation sites (SMA and FPC) and across the different experimental conditions (control, SMA TUS, and FPC TUS).
source: In fact, the standard deviation of the BOLD signal fluctuations over time were strikingly similar between the two stimulation sites (SMA and FPC, highlighted in Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and across the different experimental conditions (control, SMA TUS, and FPC TUS).
evidence: Observation about signal stability across conditions.

claim: TUS leaves intact basic haemodynamics and neurophysiology and instead has a circumscribed and specific impact on the coupling of the stimulated region with the rest of the brain.
source: This suggests that TUS leaves intact basic haemodynamics and neurophysiology and instead has a circumscribed and specific impact on the coupling of the stimulated region with the rest of the brain.
evidence: Interpretation of findings about signal properties.

claim: The presence of auditory and somatosensory confounds is likely to be a function of the specifics of the TUS protocol.
source: Third, the presence of auditory and somatosensory confounds is likely to be a function of the specifics of the TUS protocol.

claim: In sonication protocols where the ultrasound wave is pulse modulated at ~1 kHz, auditory stimulation is perhaps not unexpected.
source: In sonication protocols the ultrasound wave is often pulse modulated at ~1 kHz, well within the audible range of many rodents and primates. At these modulation frequencies auditory stimulation is perhaps not unexpected (Guo et al., 2018; Sato et al., 2018).
evidence: Explanation of auditory confound with citations.

claim: The study pulse modulated the 250 kHz ultrasound wave at 10 Hz, ensuring that the frequency of both the ultrasound wave and its modulating envelope are well outside of the macaque hearing range.
source: This is something that we have avoided in our work with macaques: we pulse modulated the 250 kHz ultrasound wave at 10 Hz: as such we ensured that the frequency of both the ultrasound wave and its modulating envelope are well outside of the macaque hearing range.
evidence: Description of protocol designed to avoid auditory confounds.

claim: The study adopted an offline experimental design where any potential audible stimulation associated with the TUS application was limited to the 40 s sonication period, while the neural activation measures were initiated tens of minutes later.
source: Moreover, here we adopted an offline experimental design where any potential audible stimulation associated with the TUS application was limited to the 40 s sonication period, while the neural activation measures were initiated tens of minutes later.
evidence: Description of temporal separation to control for auditory effects.

claim: The specificity of the results strengthens the suggestion that it might not be possible to explain away the current findings as the result of an auditory artefact having occurred up to two hours earlier.
source: Furthermore, the specificity of our results strengthens the suggestion that it might not be possible to explain away the current findings as the result of an auditory artefact having occurred up to two hours earlier.
evidence: Argument against auditory confound based on spatial and temporal specificity.

claim: The effects of TUS on SMA and FPC coupling patterns, as quantified in their connectional fingerprints, could not be explained by a potential impact of TUS on A1 activity coupling.
source: The effects of TUS on SMA and FPC coupling patterns, as quantified in their connectional fingerprints, could not be explained by a potential impact of TUS on A1 activity coupling.

claim: TUS did not affect A1 activity coupling with SMA fingerprint targets.
source: In fact, TUS did not affect A1 activity coupling with SMA fingerprint targets (Figure 5g; non-parametric permutation tests, SMA TUS: p=0.8234, FPC TUS p=0.3452), nor its coupling with FPC fingerprint targets (Figure 5h; non-parametric permutation tests, SMA TUS: p=0.5411, FPC TUS p=0.2667).

claim: TUS did not affect A1 activity coupling with FPC fingerprint targets.
source: In fact, TUS did not affect A1 activity coupling with SMA fingerprint targets (Figure 5g; non-parametric permutation tests, SMA TUS: p=0.8234, FPC TUS p=0.3452), nor its coupling with FPC fingerprint targets (Figure 5h; non-parametric permutation tests, SMA TUS: p=0.5411, FPC TUS p=0.2667).

claim: Neither SMA nor FPC changed its coupling with A1 as a function of TUS.
source: Moreover, neither SMA nor FPC changed its coupling with A1 as a function of TUS (Figure 5i; main effect of TUS: F(1,8)=0.015445, p=0.90416, d = 0.03583, CI=[−0.41483 0.46209]; interaction of TUS x connectivity seed: F(1,8)=0.18284, p=0.68022, d = 0.1234, CI=[−0.25058 0.36466]).
evidence: Statistical findings about coupling with auditory cortex.

claim: The ability of ultrasound to reversibly interact with biological tissue is not limited to grey matter.
source: The ability of ultrasound to reversibly interact with biological tissue is not limited to grey matter.

claim: The ultrasonic beam, placed over the central midline to target SMA or FPC in both hemispheres simultaneously, was likely to reach the meningeal compartment in the interhemispheric fissure.
source: We were aware that our ultrasonic beam, placed over the central midline to target SMA or FPC in both hemispheres simultaneously, was also likely to reach the meningeal compartment in the interhemispheric fissure.

claim: Ultrasound protocols designed to induce vasodilation or to temporally open the blood-brain-barrier are conventionally markedly distinct from those employed in this study, for example using higher intensities or supplemented with intravenously injected microbubbles.
source: Ultrasound protocols designed to induce vasodilation or to temporally open the blood-brain-barrier are conventionally markedly distinct from those employed here, for example using higher intensities or supplemented with intravenously injected microbubbles.

claim: A principal component analysis of the signal in the meningeal and grey matter compartments revealed the main components in either compartment explained significantly more variance following TUS compared to control.
source: A principal component analysis of the signal in the meningeal and grey matter compartments revealed the main components in either compartment explained significantly more variance following TUS compared to control (Figure 6c; main effect of TUS: F(1,9)=30.6, p=0.00036, d = 0.67031, CI=[2.1916 5.3343]; in grey matter: F(1,4)=10.743, p=0.0306, d = 1.3381, CI=[0.47735 5.7655]; in meningeal compartment: F(1,4)=16.263, p=0.0157, d = 1.6464, CI=[1.3379 7.2512]).

claim: After TUS the BOLD signal became more homogenous.
source: This observation suggests that after TUS the BOLD signal became more homogenous.

claim: The impact of TUS does not exhibit a global signal coupling effect, as illustrated by the specificity of the TUS effects for SMA and FPC.
source: However, the impact of TUS presented above does not seem to exhibit this effect, as illustrated by the specificity of the TUS effects for SMA and FPC (Figures 3,5), and further underpinned by the absence of TUS effects in regions remote from the stimulation sites (for example, Figure 6a,d illustrates the case of the posterior parietal operculum, POp).
evidence: Argument about specificity despite global signal changes.

claim: SMA TUS induced broad changes in BOLD signal even in the meningeal compartment.
source: This was because SMA TUS induced broad changes in BOLD signal even in the meningeal compartment, captured in a principal component analysis (c).

claim: These widespread TUS-induced meningeal signal coupling persisted over time for more than 1 hr after stimulation had ended.
source: These effects of TUS on widespread coupling mediated by meningeal signal persisted over time for more than 1 hr after stimulation had ended (Figure 6g).

claim: Similar effects of TUS on meningeal signal were also observed after FPC TUS.
source: Similar effects of TUS on meningeal signal were also observed after FPC TUS (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Replication of meningeal effects for different target.

claim: In unconfounded fMRI data FPC TUS did not have a strong impact outside the stimulated region.
source: We note that in unconfounded fMRI data FPC TUS did not have a strong impact outside the stimulated region (illustrated for POp in Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Finding about spatial specificity in properly processed data.

claim: In fMRI data confounded by meningeal-driven global nuisance, FPC stimulation led to widespread enhanced signal coupling compared to the control state.
source: In contrast, in fMRI data confounded by meningeal-driven global nuisance, FPC stimulation led to widespread enhanced signal coupling compared to the control state.
evidence: Finding about global effects in confounded data.

claim: The effect of FPC TUS on meningeal signal was replicated in a new set of animals in experiment 3.
source: This effect of FPC TUS was replicated in a new set of animals in experiment 3 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claim: TUS over the medial meningeal compartment may produce widespread changes that are non-neuronal in origin.
source: Although the effect was perhaps not as strong as that seen after SMA TUS, this finding again suggests that TUS over the medial meningeal compartment may produce widespread changes that are non-neuronal in origin.

claim: Differences in morphology of the sagittal sinus along the rostro-caudal axis might explain the weakened global effect after FPC TUS compared to SMA TUS.
source: Differences in morphology of the sagittal sinus along the rostro-caudal axis might explain this weakened global effect.
evidence: Speculative explanation for differences between targets.

claim: Some higher intensity ultrasound stimulation protocols have been shown to induce thermal lesions or haemorrhage following cavitation.
source: Some higher intensity ultrasound stimulation protocols, distinct from those used here, have been shown to induce thermal lesions or haemorrhage following cavitation (Elias et al., 2013).
evidence: Prior finding about high-intensity protocols with citation.

claim: No structural changes resembling those seen with higher intensity ultrasound protocols were observed despite 40 s trains of TUS inducing sustained changes in the post-stimulation period.
source: Despite the fact that 40 s trains of TUS induced sustained changes in the post-stimulation period in experiments 1 and 2, no structural changes remotely resembling those seen with higher intensity ultrasound protocols were observed.

claim: No indication of TUS-induced oedema was observed when comparing T1w MRI structural scans collected in baseline sessions with T1w scans collected after TUS.
source: First of all, we did not observe any indication of TUS-induced oedema when comparing T1w MRI structural scans collected in baseline sessions with T1w scans collected after TUS (Figure 7).

claim: No tissue alteration (e.g. tissue burn) was observed at the post-mortem examination.
source: We also did not observe tissue alteration (e.g. tissue burn) at the post-mortem examination.

claim: No signs of neuronal alteration or haemorrhage were observed in histological analyses of three macaques following pre-SMA TUS.
source: Neither were any signs of neuronal alteration or haemorrhage observed in histological analyses of three macaques following pre-SMA TUS (Figure 8).

claim: The maximum spatial-peak pulse-averaged intensity (Isppa) at the acoustic focus point was 24.1 W/cm2 for the SMA target and 31.7 W/cm2 for the FPC target.
source: As estimated by these numerical simulations, the maximum spatial-peak pulse-averaged intensity (Isppa) at the acoustic focus point was 24.1 W/cm2 for the SMA target and 31.7 W/cm2 for the FPC target (spatial peak temporal average intensities, Ispta: 7.2 W/cm2 and 9.5 W/cm2 for SMA and FPC, respectively).

claim: The spatial peak temporal average intensities (Ispta) were 7.2 W/cm2 for SMA and 9.5 W/cm2 for FPC.
source: As estimated by these numerical simulations, the maximum spatial-peak pulse-averaged intensity (Isppa) at the acoustic focus point was 24.1 W/cm2 for the SMA target and 31.7 W/cm2 for the FPC target (spatial peak temporal average intensities, Ispta: 7.2 W/cm2 and 9.5 W/cm2 for SMA and FPC, respectively).

claim: The skull is more acoustically absorbing than soft tissue.
source: Given that the skull is more acoustically absorbing than soft tissue, the highest thermal increase is located in the skull itself, estimated by the simulation to be 2.9°C.
evidence: Physical property stated in context of thermal modeling.

claim: The highest thermal increase is located in the skull itself, estimated by the simulation to be 2.9°C.
source: Given that the skull is more acoustically absorbing than soft tissue, the highest thermal increase is located in the skull itself, estimated by the simulation to be 2.9°C.

claim: The maximum temperature below the dura was 38.0°C.
source: Given an approximate 0.5 mm thickness of the dura (Galashan et al., 2011) the maximum temperature below the dura was 38.0°C.
evidence: Result from thermal simulation with citation for dura thickness.

claim: The maximal thermal increase at the geometrical focus of the sonic transducer was less than 0.5°C.
source: The maximal thermal increase at the geometrical focus of the sonic transducer was less than 0.5°C (Figure 2).

claim: The study demonstrates a protocol for transcranial focused ultrasound stimulation (TUS) that can induce a sustained yet reversible change in neural activity.
source: In this study we demonstrate a protocol for transcranial focused ultrasound stimulation (TUS) that can induce a sustained yet reversible change in neural activity.

claim: Each brain area's unique contribution to cognition and behaviour is shaped by how activity in each area is a function of a unique fingerprint of interconnected areas.
source: We focused our investigation on modulations of brain connectivity, following the notion that each brain area's unique contribution to cognition and behaviour is shaped by how activity in each area is a function of a unique fingerprint of interconnected areas (Passingham et al., 2002).

claim: Each area's connectional fingerprint was significantly changed by TUS, but only when it was applied to that area itself.
source: We found that each area's connectional fingerprint was significantly changed by TUS, but only when it was applied to that area itself (Figures 3,5).
evidence: Summary of main finding with figure references.

claim: The changes observed might be summarized as more uniform activation in the stimulated region combined with a sharpening of the normal coupling pattern that each area has even at rest.
source: The changes observed might be summarized as more uniform activation in the stimulated region combined with a sharpening of the normal coupling pattern that each area has even at rest.

claim: Activity coupling with strongly interconnected areas, which are often nearby, was increased but activity coupling with less strongly connected regions was reduced.
source: Activity coupling with strongly interconnected areas, which are often nearby, was increased but activity coupling with less strongly connected regions was reduced.

claim: Such changes in connectional fingerprints might constitute the mechanism by which TUS is able to induce regionally specific patterns of behavioural change when applied in awake behaving animals.
source: Such changes in connectional fingerprints might constitute the mechanism by which TUS is able to induce regionally specific patterns of behavioural change when applied in awake behaving animals (Deffieux et al., 2013; Fouragnan et al., 2019).
evidence: Proposed mechanistic link to behavior with citations.

claim: The pattern of inputs each area receives from other areas and the influence it wields over other areas are a major determinant of its function.
source: The pattern of inputs each area receives from other areas and the influence it wields over other areas are a major determinant of its function and here we have shown that this pattern is altered by TUS.

claim: TUS may provide a relatively straightforward method for sustained but reversible manipulation of specific components of neural circuits in the primate brain.
source: TUS may therefore provide a relatively straightforward method for sustained but reversible manipulation of specific components of neural circuits in the primate brain (Wattiez et al., 2017).
evidence: Conclusion about TUS utility with citation.

claim: TUS may be important for investigating primate brain areas when homologues in non-primate species, such as rodents, are non-existent or disputed.
source: This may be important for investigating primate brain areas when homologues in non-primate species, such as rodents, are non-existent or disputed (Preuss, 1995; Wise, 2008).

claim: This work paves the way for the development and use of offline TUS protocols in primates, including humans, both as a research tool and as potential clinical intervention.
source: This work paves the way for the development and use of offline TUS protocols in primates, including humans, both as a research tool and as potential clinical intervention.

claim: TUS application produced different effects when applied to SMA versus FPC.
source: In experiments 1 and 2, adopting a within-subject design with three animals, we found that TUS application produced different effects when applied to different brain regions: the SMA, a part of motor association cortex, and FPC a part of granular prefrontal cortex (Figures 3,5).

claim: In each case the TUS effects were prominent within the connectional fingerprint of the area stimulated.
source: However, in each case the TUS effects were prominent within the connectional fingerprint of the area stimulated.

claim: The connectional fingerprints of SMA and FPC are distinct.
source: The connectional fingerprints of SMA and FPC are distinct (Johansen-Berg et al., 2004; Neubert et al., 2014; Sallet et al., 2013).
evidence: Characterization of brain regions with citations.

claim: The effects of TUS are regionally specific.
source: The effects of TUS are thus regionally specific.

claim: TUS can be used as a neuromodulatory technique that allows one to non-surgically target cortical and subcortical brain areas with superior spatial specificity and depth of stimulation compared to other transcranial stimulation approaches.
source: Our results confirm that TUS can be used as a neuromodulatory technique that allows one to non-surgically target cortical and subcortical brain areas with superior spatial specificity and depth of stimulation (Folloni et al., 2019) compared to other transcranial stimulation approaches (e.g. TMS and TCS; Bestmann and Walsh, 2017; Dayan et al., 2013; Polanía et al., 2018).
evidence: Conclusion about TUS advantages with citations.

claim: It is not easy to use invasive techniques like electrical microstimulation to disrupt activity in all areas especially when they are not somatotopically mapped.
source: While successes have been achieved with some invasive techniques, such as electrical microstimulation (Krug et al., 2015; Vanduffel, 2016), it is not easy to use them to disrupt activity in all areas especially when they are not somatotopically mapped.
evidence: Limitation of alternative techniques with citations.

claim: The spatially specific effects observed after TUS cannot be attributed to any common auditory impact that occurs at the time of stimulation.
source: The spatially specific effects that we observed after TUS cannot, however, be attributed to any common auditory impact that occurs at the time of stimulation.

claim: In order to avoid both the confounding effect associated with the sound of TUS and interference of the ultrasonic wave field with fMRI measurement, an 'offline' stimulation protocol was used.
source: Moreover, in order to avoid both the confounding effect associated with the sound of TUS and interference of the ultrasonic wave field with fMRI measurement, we opted for an 'offline' stimulation protocol.

claim: Stimulation was a 40 s train that ended at least 20 min before the fMRI data acquisition period.
source: Stimulation was a 40 s train that ended at least 20 min before the fMRI data acquisition period.

claim: The sustained nature of the train and other features of the stimulation pulses may make the protocol used here more effective for neuromodulation, while ensuring the thermal modulation of the cortex remains limited (<1°C).
source: The sustained nature of the train and other features of the stimulation pulses may make the protocol used here more effective for neuromodulation, while ensuring the thermal modulation of the cortex remains limited (<1°C, Figure 2).
evidence: Proposed advantage of protocol with thermal constraint.

claim: Limited thermal changes (<1°C) are not associated with neuromodulatory effects observed more than 30 min after the stimulation.
source: Such limited thermal changes are not associated with neuromodulatory effects observed more than 30 min after the stimulation: the thermal rise is short-lived (Dallapiazza et al., 2018), not accompanied by tissue damage and below the thermal effects observed with some protocols in rodents (for a review, see Constans et al., 2018).
evidence: Argument that thermal effects don't explain sustained neuromodulation with citations.

claim: When TUS was applied to FPC in three other individuals in experiment 3, it induced spatially specific effects similar to those seen in experiment 2.
source: In experiment 3 we found that TUS had reproducible effects. When TUS was applied to FPC in three other individuals, it induced spatially specific effects similar to those seen in experiment 2.

claim: The effects of the non-invasive 40 s stimulation protocol are sustained and lasted over much of the two-hour period investigated.
source: The effects of the non-invasive 40 s stimulation protocol used here are sustained and lasted over much of the two-hour period we investigated.
evidence: Summary of temporal extent of effects.

claim: These effects are more extended than those produced by other techniques commonly used for offline disruption of cortical activity such as TMS.
source: These effects are more extended than those produced by other techniques commonly used for offline disruption of cortical activity such as TMS (Huang et al., 2005; O'Shea et al., 2007).
evidence: Comparison with alternative technique with citations.

claim: Care should be taken in using the technique in human cognitive neuroscience experiments as TUS effects may continue beyond the short periods that participants typically spend within the laboratory.
source: Care should therefore be taken in using the technique in human cognitive neuroscience experiments; TUS effects may continue beyond the short periods that participants typically spend within the laboratory.
evidence: Caution for human application based on sustained effects.

claim: It may be important to carefully characterize the time course of TUS effects in animal models before their use with human participants.
source: It may therefore be important to carefully characterize the time course of TUS effects in animal models before their use with human participants.

claim: Some caution might be warranted in relation to the potential of ultrasound to cause microstructural damage, especially when stimulating at higher intensities, longer durations, or for more repetitions.
source: Some caution might also be warranted in relation to the potential of ultrasound to cause microstructural damage, especially when stimulating at higher intensities, longer durations, or for more repetitions.

claim: The structural MRI and histological analyses did not reveal any evidence of damage and were comparable to previous studies.
source: While our structural MRI and histological analyses did not reveal any evidence of damage and were comparable to previous studies (Dallapiazza et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2016b), it would be of interest in the future to include additional histological indices of apoptotic or inflammatory processes (Tufail et al., 2010) to further assess the safety of TUS.
evidence: Safety finding with citations and suggestion for future work.

claim: The thermal modelling approach was designed to estimate an informed upper-bound on potential thermal effects.
source: Similarly, the thermal modelling approach we adopted here was designed to estimate an informed upper-bound on potential thermal effects, but when further developing this protocol additional simulation validations – for example based on phantom measurements – might be informative.
evidence: Description of modeling approach and suggestion for validation.

claim: In addition to the spatially specific effects of TUS, changes in the BOLD signal originating from the meningeal compartment were observed that were not specific to the area stimulated.
source: In addition to the spatially specific effects of TUS we also observed changes in the BOLD signal originating from the meningeal compartment that were not specific to the area stimulated.

claim: Similar meningeal effects were seen each time either the SMA or FPC was stimulated, but the effect was generally more pronounced after SMA stimulation than after FPC stimulation.
source: Although similar effects were seen each time either the SMA or FPC was stimulated, the effect was generally more pronounced after SMA stimulation than after FPC stimulation.
evidence: Comparison of meningeal effects between targets.

claim: Preliminary results from TUS of other brain areas suggest that spatially non-specific effects may be even smaller when TUS is applied elsewhere.
source: Our preliminary results from TUS of other brain areas suggest that these spatially non-specific effects may be even smaller when TUS is applied elsewhere (Folloni et al., 2019).

claim: It is possible that non-specific effects may result from a direct vascular effect of TUS as the sagittal sinus is directly above the midline frontal regions that were targeted.
source: While the precise origin of the non-specific effects was difficult to determine it is possible that they may result from a direct vascular effect of TUS; the sagittal sinus is directly above the midline frontal regions that we targeted and is included in the meningeal compartment during MRI analysis protocols.

claim: The presence of non-specific effects underlines the need for care in translating the technique to humans, especially when the targeted region is near venous sinuses or cerebral arteries.
source: The presence of such non-specific effects again underlines the need for care in translating the technique to humans; especially when the targeted region is near venous sinuses or cerebral arteries.

claim: Non-specific effects underline the need for comparing the behavioural effects of TUS not just with a non-stimulation sham condition but with TUS application to another control brain region.
source: In addition, they underline the need for comparing the behavioural effects of TUS not just with a non-stimulation sham condition but with TUS application to another control brain region.

claim: The absence of marked histological changes in experiment 4 provides one important safety benchmark and confirms previous histological results in lagomorphs.
source: The absence of marked histological changes in experiment 4, however, provides one important safety benchmark and confirms previous histological results in lagomorphs (Yoo et al., 2011).
evidence: Safety finding with citation to prior work.

claim: Combining TUS and fMRI is a promising approach to overcome the restrictions of each of the individual techniques.
source: Combining TUS and fMRI is a promising approach to overcome the restrictions of each of the individual techniques.

claim: TUS has a detectable offline and sustained impact on the distinctive network of connectivity associated with the stimulated brain region – the connectional fingerprint.
source: Here we have shown that TUS has a detectable offline and sustained impact on the distinctive network of connectivity associated with the stimulated brain region – the connectional fingerprint.

claim: A brain region's interactions with other regions – its unique connectional fingerprint or specific pattern of inputs and outputs – are an important determinant of its functional role.
source: A brain region's interactions with other regions – its unique connectional fingerprint or specific pattern of inputs and outputs – are an important determinant of its functional role.

claim: The current results are consistent with TUS application exerting regionally specific effects on behaviour.
source: The current results are therefore consistent with TUS application exerting regionally specific effects on behaviour (Deffieux et al., 2013; Fouragnan et al., 2019).
evidence: Interpretation linking findings to behavior with citations.

claim: The fact that fMRI allows the effects of TUS to be studied with a high spatial resolution suggests the TUS-fMRI combination has the potential to become a powerful neuroscientific tool.
source: The fact that fMRI allows the effects of TUS to be studied with a high spatial resolution suggests the TUS-fMRI combination has the potential to become a powerful neuroscientific tool.
evidence: Conclusion about future potential of combined method.

claim: Six healthy male macaques (Macaca mulatta) were stimulated with transcranial focused ultrasound and scanned to acquire resting state functional magnetic resonance images (rs-fMRI) and anatomical MR images.
source: For this study, six healthy male macaques (Macaca mulatta, NCBITaxon:9544) were stimulated with transcranial focused ultrasound and scanned to acquire resting state functional magnetic resonance images (rs-fMRI) and anatomical MR images.

claim: Three animals participated in experiment 1 [SMA TUS] with mean age and weight at time of scan: 5.6 years, 10.7 kg.
source: Three animals participated in experiment 1 [SMA TUS] (all males, mean age and weight at time of scan: 5.6 years, 10.7 kg).

claim: The same three animals participated in experiment 2 [FPC TUS] at time of scan: 6.1 years, 11.8 kg.
source: The same three animals participated in experiment 2 [FPC TUS] (at time of scan: 6.1 years, 11.8 kg), and the control condition (at time of scan: 5.5 years, 10.2 kg).

claim: Three different animals participated in experiment 3 [FPC TUS validation] with mean age and weight at time of scan: 10.3 years, 13 kg.
source: Three different animals participated in experiment 3 [FPC TUS validation] (all males, mean age and weight at time of scan: 10.3 years, 13 kg).

claim: Six animals were included in the histology analysis (experiment 4): three control animals who did not receive TUS and three pre-SMA TUS animals post stimulation.
source: In addition to this set of animals, six animals were included in the histology analysis (experiment 4): three control animals who did not receive TUS (two females; mean age and weight at time of perfusion: 9.3 years, 9.1 kg) and three pre-SMA TUS animals post stimulation (all males; mean age and weight at time of perfusion: 8.4 years, 13.1 kg).

claim: All procedures were conducted under licenses from the United Kingdom (UK) Home Office in accordance with The Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act 1986.
source: All procedures were conducted under licenses from the United Kingdom (UK) Home Office in accordance with The Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act 1986.

claim: All procedures complied with the European Union guidelines (EU Directive 2010/63/EU).
source: In all cases they complied with the European Union guidelines (EU Directive 2010/63/EU).

claim: A single element ultrasound transducer (H115-MR, diameter 64 mm, Sonic Concept) with 51.74 mm focal depth was used.
source: A single element ultrasound transducer (H115-MR, diameter 64 mm, Sonic Concept, Bothell, WA, USA) with 51.74 mm focal depth was used with a coupling cone filled with degassed water and sealed with a latex membrane (Durex).

claim: The resonance frequency of the ultrasonic wave was set at 250 kHz with 30 ms bursts of ultrasound generated every 100 ms.
source: The resonance frequency of the ultrasonic wave was set at 250 kHz with 30 ms bursts of ultrasound generated every 100 ms, controlled through a digital function generator (Handyscope HS5, TiePie engineering, Sneek, The Netherlands).

claim: The stimulation lasted for 40 s.
source: The stimulation lasted for 40 s.

claim: A 75-Watt amplifier was used to deliver the required power to the transducer.
source: A 75-Watt amplifier (75A250A, Amplifier Research, Souderton, PA) was used to deliver the required power to the transducer.

claim: Voltage values per session ranged from 130 to 142 V, corresponding to 1.17 to 1.35 MPa as measured in water.
source: The recorded peak-to-peak voltage was kept constant throughout the stimulation. Voltage values per session ranged from 130 to 142 V, corresponding to 1.17 to 1.35 MPa as measured in water with an in house heterodyne interferometer (Constans et al., 2017).
evidence: Measurement of stimulation parameters with citation.

claim: Each of the areas targeted in experiments 1–4 lie close to the midline.
source: Each of the areas targeted in experiments 1–4 lie close to the midline. Therefore, we applied a single train over the midline stimulating the target region in both hemispheres simultaneously.

claim: A single train was applied over the midline stimulating the target region in both hemispheres simultaneously.
source: Each of the areas targeted in experiments 1–4 lie close to the midline. Therefore, we applied a single train over the midline stimulating the target region in both hemispheres simultaneously.

claim: TUS was guided using a frameless stereotaxic neuronavigation system set up for each animal individually by registering a T1-weighted MR image to the animal's head.
source: In order to direct TUS to the target region, we guided the stimulation using a frameless stereotaxic neuronavigation system (Rogue Research, Montreal, CA; RRID:SCR_009539) set up for each animal individually by registering a T1-weighted MR image to the animal's head.

claim: Positions of both the ultrasound transducer and the head of the animal were tracked continuously with infrared reflectors to inform online and accurate positioning of the transducer over the targeted brain region.
source: Positions of both the ultrasound transducer and the head of the animal were tracked continuously with infrared reflectors to inform online and accurate positioning of the transducer over the targeted brain region: SMA in experiment 1, (Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) X, Y, and Z coordinates in mm [0.1 2 19]); FPC in experiment 2 [0.6 24 10]; FPC in experiment 3 [-0.7 24 11]; pre-SMA in experiment 4 [0.2 11 17].
evidence: Description of tracking system and target coordinates.

claim: The ultrasound transducer/coupling cone montage was placed directly onto previously shaved skin prepared with conductive gel to ensure ultrasonic coupling between the transducer and the animal's scalp.
source: The ultrasound transducer/coupling cone montage was placed directly onto previously shaved skin prepared with conductive gel (SignaGel Electrode; Parker Laboratories Inc.) to ensure ultrasonic coupling between the transducer and the animal's scalp.

claim: In the non-stimulation condition (control), all procedures (anaesthesia, pre-scan preparation, fMRI scan acquisition and timing), with the exception of actual TUS, matched the TUS sessions.
source: In the non-stimulation condition (control), all procedures (anaesthesia, pre-scan preparation, fMRI scan acquisition and timing), with the exception of actual TUS, matched the TUS sessions.

claim: The acoustic wave propagation was simulated using a k-space pseudospectral method-based solver, k-Wave.
source: The acoustic wave propagation of our focused ultrasound protocol (at 130 V peak-to-peak voltage) was simulated using a k-space pseudospectral method-based solver, k-Wave (Cox et al., 2007) to obtain estimates for the pressure amplitude, peak intensity, spatial distribution, and thermal impact at steady state.
evidence: Description of simulation method with citation.

claim: 3D maps of the skull were extracted from a monkey CT scan.
source: 3D maps of the skull were extracted from a monkey CT scan (Kyoto University online database, ID 1478, 0.26 mm isotropic resolution).

claim: Soft tissues were assumed to be homogeneous, with acoustic values of water (ρtissue =1000 kg/m3 and ctissue =1500 m/s).
source: Soft tissues were assumed to be homogeneous, with acoustic values of water (ρtissue =1000 kg/m3 and ctissue =1500 m/s).

claim: The ultrasound sonication and subsequent MRI scans were performed under inhalational isoflurane gas anaesthesia using a protocol which has previously proven successful in preserving whole-brain functional connectivity as measured with BOLD signal.
source: The ultrasound sonication and subsequent MRI scans were performed under inhalational isoflurane gas anaesthesia using a protocol which has previously proven successful in preserving whole-brain functional connectivity as measured with BOLD signal (Mars et al., 2013; Mars et al., 2011; Neubert et al., 2015; Neubert et al., 2014; O'Reilly et al., 2013; Sallet et al., 2013; Vincent et al., 2007).
evidence: Description of anaesthesia protocol with citations justifying its use.
